body.text: This year, while Indo-US relations have been marred by an unpredictable White House, India has made significant headway with Europe. Besides concluding the India-Europe Free Trade Agreement (FTA), New Delhi has entered into “Strategic Partnerships” with two Nordic countries, Sweden and Finland (which share a 1,340 km border with Russia). These partnerships signal an era of strategic autonomy with alliances accommodating conflicting interests.
To better understand the evolving partnership between New Delhi and Helsinki, and the changing dynamics in Europe, Frontline spoke to the new Finland Ambassador to India, Mikko Kivikoski.
The relationship between India and Finland has seen significant momentum recently. How would you describe this wave of engagement?

We have witnessed record-high engagements this year. In February, our Prime Minister Petteri Orpo visited India for the AI Impact Summit. Our President Alexander Stubb paid a state visit in March, during which Finland and India elevated the bilateral relationship to a “Strategic Partnership in Digitalization and Sustainability”.

In May, Prime Minister Narendra Modi attended the Nordic-India Summit in Oslo. In June, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar [visited], and then Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal visited Finland in July. In September, the World Circular Economy Forum (a Finnish initiative) was held in Gandhinagar, Gujarat. This was the forum’s 10th edition and the first time it was held in South Asia. Our Minister for the Environment and Climate, Sari Multala, attended and held bilateral meetings. There is real momentum building.

Besides these bilateral visits, the European Union Commission was in India earlier this year, and the two sides agreed to add defence and security as another element of the strategic partnership. They also concluded the EU-India FTA, which is expected to be signed in Brussels in December.
You said India is being “rediscovered” in Finland. What has India done to capture Finnish imagination?

One major reason Europeans and Indians, Finns and Indians, are getting closer is geopolitics. Everybody now wants strategic autonomy, supply chains, and partnerships. You cannot do everything by yourself; you need trusted partners. Minister Goyal recently said at the Berlin Global Dialogue that trust is becoming the “new rare earth”. That is very neatly put. We see India, the EU, and Finland as trusted partners. Five years ago, you could hardly find news about India in Finnish newspapers. Now, whenever you open a paper, there is news on India.
Apart from political visits, has anything concrete happened on the ground? These announcements often take a long time to materialise.

New Finnish companies are actively entering the Indian market. I cannot as yet disclose the details, but negotiations are under way on several major projects. Take Nokia, which now works primarily in networks, and ICEYE, a (Finnish) satellite company. They recently announced a collaboration on satellite communication systems, offering a dual-use system. It can be used in natural disasters when 5G networks break down, or for border management, and also for military purposes.
How is it different from Starlink?

Unlike in the case of Starlink, there will be full sovereign control over the system. Nokia-ICEYE are offering governments a dual-use satellite communication system. Once a government buys the system, it has full control over it.
What can a small country like Finland offer to India, and vice versa?

We have a population of just 5.5 million, just one-sixth of Delhi’s. But we are a major player in technology and solutions, while India has scale and talent. When you combine the two, the future looks promising.
Apart from being a huge market, what else can India offer?
You clearly have scale.
We hear about scale all the time. India cannot simply be a market to sell products.

No, no. You have scale and talent. We are now moving towards partnership and two-way engagement. Earlier, it was simply a matter of buying and selling. The relationship is more comprehensive now. I would emphasise the word “partnership”. It is not only about trade; it is about investment and people-to-people contact.
Finnish research in semiconductors could also be useful to India since it wants to reduce its dependence on China.
It could be. I think we are all seeking strategic autonomy and more reliable supply chains. For that, we need to join forces. There is more that unites us than what divides us.
What hurdles do European and Finnish businesses face in India?

Companies that are doing well here are quite pleased. They recognise that the business environment can still be challenging, but the opportunities are huge. Big companies are willing to take that risk, but small and medium-sized businesses are cautious. My biggest task is to convince them that now is the time to come to India. If they wait, they will miss the train.

You spoke about trust. India is extremely close to your largest neighbour, Russia. Finland joined NATO following Russia’s attack on Ukraine. How do you manage this complicated relationship with India?

There are historical reasons, too. In 1939, the Soviet Union attacked us. We fought back and lost, and were forced to sign a peace agreement conceding 10 per cent of our territory and paying heavy reparations. But we preserved our independence and sovereignty.
How do you see the Russian war against Ukraine unfolding?

A solution will not be found on the battlefield. Over the last month, the Ukrainians have gained more territory. When neither side can win on the battlefield, the only solution is negotiation. Both sides will have to make compromises. The Ukrainians are signalling that they are willing to negotiate and compromise.
Does that mean conceding some territory?

No. But they understand that in this kind of situation you cannot make maximalist demands. The Russians, however, are still making such demands. They are not showing any willingness even to a ceasefire.
We need to create incentives for the Russians to change their calculations. Europe will continue supporting Ukraine while increasing pressure on Russia through sanctions and other means.
A year ago it seemed that without the US, Europe would find it difficult to support Ukraine against Russia. What is the situation now?

The war has gone on for longer than the First and Second World Wars. Everybody wants it to end because the consequences are enormous. You feel them in India, too. Your External Affairs Minister has spoken about the impact.
How do you assess the role of the US in this situation?
The US has the strongest military in the world. It is important that the US remains engaged in finding a solution.
Given the unpredictability of the White House, do you think it will take credible steps to restore peace?

The Americans are working towards peace all the time. Recently, the US special envoy, Steve Witkoff, met the Ukrainians in Oslo and then Russians in St. Petersburg. The Americans are heavily involved. We all know that [US] President Donald Trump wants to end the war.
I would not comment on that. What we need is for the global community to put pressure on Putin and bring him to the negotiating table.
You have served in Russia and Kazakhstan, a former Soviet republic. What was your experience?

I have been posted to Russia twice, in Moscow and St. Petersburg. When I was in St. Petersburg, we were issuing 1.2 million visas to Russians annually. 80 per cent of them were multi-year visas. At the same time, there were 20 million border crossings. We had extensive interaction at every level, from the highest political levels to civil society.
When was this?

I was in St. Petersburg from 2014 to 2017, and in Moscow from 2002 to 2005. Those were the years when we believed, and the Russians also believed, that greater cooperation would benefit both sides. Since the end of the Cold War, we had invested a great deal in building a mutually beneficial relationship with Russia.

The attack on Ukraine was a huge disappointment for us. I have personally spent several years of my career working towards a better relationship. Now trust has been completely lost, and it will take time to rebuild it.
How has the attack on Ukraine impacted Finland?
Russia’s war has had a relatively limited economic impact on Finland because we were not dependent on Russian energy. We have cut our dependencies on Russia. Trade with Russia is minimal today.

Having said that, we are neighbours. Finland and Russia share a 1,340 km border. We will remain neighbours. At some point, we will have to manage the bilateral relationship. But that requires Russia to stop the war.
In the aftermath of the Russian aggression, how has Finland upgraded its military?

Not much, because we never scaled down our military after the Second World War. Many other European countries thought history was over after the Cold War, and cut spending. Finland did not do that. We maintained our conscription system. My youngest son is 20 and is currently doing his mandatory military service. I have done it, my father did it, and my grandfather did it and fought against the Soviets.
A European diplomat once told me that the Finns had been the smartest people in Europe. You maintained your military supplies during the Cold War and thereafter.

We currently have one of the strongest armies in Europe and one of the largest artillery capabilities. With a population of just 5.5 million, we can mobilise 280,000 people in a few days and close to a million within a few weeks.
What have been your expectations from India? How do you find its efforts to bring the war to an end?

I will not offer recommendations to the Indian government, but all of India’s efforts are appreciated. India has a special position because its diplomatic channels are open both to Moscow and to Kyiv. As the world’s largest democracy and a leading voice of the Global South, what India says and does have a massive impact.
Coming to the Indo-Finland relationship, what place do ordinary people occupy in this relationship? Several Western states now appear hostile to communities from the Global South.

People are at the centre. More than 30,000 Indians live permanently in Finland, mostly working as a highly respected community in the ICT [information and communications technology] sector. We also have around 3,000 Indian students in Finnish universities, and that number is growing.
Europe needs skilled workers, yet there is a massive backlash against migrants. How is Finland balancing this?
Europe’s population is ageing rapidly, and we need workers to keep services running. Finland and India signed a migration and mobility agreement, and we explicitly welcome skilled workers.
Migration is a highly sensitive political issue because integration hasn’t succeeded in every case, which is partly the reason why we are seeing protests.
How do you see the ongoing protests in Europe?
Peaceful protest is part of democracy, of freedom of speech and expression. It’s the European way of life, but violent and criminal elements are unacceptable and must be held accountable.
Finland is repeatedly ranked the happiest country in the world. What accounts for that?
We joke about it ourselves: Why are we the happiest ones? On a serious note, I think this index is more about how individuals relate to their everyday life than about smiling all the time.

There are a few things about why the Finns are happy. One is trust. You know that you can trust your fellow countrymen and women. You can trust the institutions, authorities. Then there is a principle that no one is left behind. We have had hard times during our history, but we always believed in the principle. Trust in the family, authorities, institutions, and the duty that nobody is left behind. These are probably two of the key features which explain our happiness.
Finland also has a robust welfare system. What advice would you give to India?

We have just 5.5 million people. Trust is easier to build. Things are a little more straightforward than they are in a country of 1.5 billion. But it is not guaranteed that the welfare model will last forever. It costs an enormous amount of money.
It also creates resentment?
It does. European economies are not doing particularly well. In Finland, we are debating how we can afford the welfare system.
When we gained independence in 1917, after the First World War, we were one of the poorest countries in Europe. Our only natural resource was forests. Essentially, we had only people and forests.
And forests in Finland are now being cleared for data centres. Your government recently prohibited Microsoft from felling forests.
Microsoft was planning to build a data centre, but the necessary permits were not in place.
As you begin your official stint in India, your first in South Asia, what is your agenda? What would you like to go back with?

I want to significantly advance the bilateral relationship by driving more trade and more people-to-people contact. Secondly, I want to see the EU-India FTA successfully finalised and brought into force.
Ashutosh Bhardwaj is an independent writer and journalist.
